rows: The principal eyes of a jumping spider are the sharp pair in front. The best measured figure, for Portia, resolves about 12.4 cycles per degree, close to a person's sharpness. Most other measured jumping spiders are far blunter, at about 3.8 cycles per degree in Phidippus johnsoni.
A narrow strip, moved to look

Each principal eye sees only a thin upright strip, about 2 degrees wide and about 21 degrees high in Phidippus johnsoni. The spider moves its retinas across the scene to build a view, so the sharp part is narrow.

The side eyes see much wider. In Phidippus audax the front side eye covers about 70 degrees across and 98 degrees up, and in Metaphidippus aeneolus the side eyes between them cover almost the whole circle around the animal.
The principal eyes see ultraviolet and green. In Plexippus validus, UV cells peak at 360 nm and green cells at about 520 nm. Some species differ, and the view draws the two classes.
The side eyes mainly detect movement. Moving things reach them more easily than still ones, and a light that only switches on and off evokes no turn in Metaphidippus harfordi.
The blur, the lingering picture, the brightness gain and the slow flicker are the app's own choices, set from the sharpness and flicker records. The sharp strip is drawn at 2 degrees by the app.

rows: In the whales and seals studied, the blue-sensitive cone is missing, so one kind of cone is left and these animals are essentially colour-blind. A bottlenose dolphin's cone peaks near 524 nanometres. Some baleen and sperm whales have also lost the cone pigments and see by rods alone. We draw colour as that single cone would give it.

Estimates of sharpness run from 1.6 cycles per degree in a manatee and 3.3 in a humpback whale to 4.8 in a Bryde's whale. A harbour seal reaches 8.7 in air and 11.5 under water. A person manages about 30. We blur the picture to about 5.

A dolphin's eyes sit on the sides of its head and give a visual field of 120 to 130 degrees, with the two eyes overlapping by only 20 to 30 degrees. A sperm whale has no overlap at all. The records give no field for seals, so we use the dolphin figure for the whole view.

A bottlenose dolphin sees half a log unit better than a person in dim light, which is about three times better, and 0.2 log units worse in bright light. Dolphins, other whales and many seals carry a reflecting layer behind the retina, while manatees have none. We lift the brightness of the picture by about three times.

Dolphins and porpoises send out clicks of 40 to 150 kilohertz and listen for the echoes. A bottlenose dolphin or sperm whale sends its sound in a beam about 8 to 9 degrees wide. A phone cannot hear or draw this, so it is left out.

A harbour seal can sense targets as far as 180 metres away by its whiskers, even when it has lost vision and hearing. It can follow the trail of a robot submarine that had a 20 second head start. No phone input matches this, so it is left out.

The records come from many species, so the app picked single numbers for the whole group: a sharpness of 5, a field of 125 degrees, a brightness lift of about three and a reflective sheen of 0.6. The mapping of colour onto one cone is also the app's.

rows: A scorpion has one pair of median eyes in the middle of its shield and three to five pairs of smaller lateral eyes at the front corners. In some species the last two pairs of lateral eyes are tiny.
Scorpions are reported to see 360 degrees around the body, with a small overlap of about 40 degrees above the animal where the two median eyes look at the same place.

Both sets of eyes are most sensitive to green light near 500 nm. The lateral eyes also have a weaker peak in the ultraviolet. This view shows one green-sensitive pigment, so the world has a single hue.

Scorpion eyes respond to starlight levels of light, which suits an animal that hides by day and hunts at night. In one desert species the median eyes are about 3 log units more sensitive at night than by day.
The median eyes are thought to give the better picture, with fairly good detail. The lateral eyes may detect only changes in light.

No one has measured how much detail a scorpion sees. This view assumes a coarse picture and a brighter night than a person would see. The squeeze of the whole circle into the screen is the app's choice.
A scorpion finds prey by feeling vibrations in the sand through its legs, up to about 50 cm away, and it tastes the ground with its comb-like pectines. The camera records neither.

rows: A bee resolves about a quarter of a cycle per degree, so it sees roughly a hundredth to a two-hundredth as much fine detail as a person. Each eye is built from about 5,400 lens facets, and the picture looks coarse and soft.

A bee has three kinds of colour receptor, tuned near 346, 430 and 540 nanometres, which are ultraviolet, blue and green. Red light is out of reach. This view shifts those three onto the screen's blue, green and red so that ultraviolet shows up as a colour a person can see.
Together the two compound eyes cover about 300 degrees around the head. Only a small blind patch lies below and behind the bee.

Bees can follow a flicker of about 100 to 200 times a second, which gives them more moments to look at each movement. This view plays time at 0.4 of normal speed as a hint of that. The figure is the app's own choice.
About a third of the flower species in one survey carry ultraviolet patterns, and a common one is a dark centre in a reflecting flower. Most of the others absorb ultraviolet all over.
The app chose to squeeze the wide field onto the screen and to map the three receptor peaks onto screen colours. Neither choice comes from a measurement.

rows: Many monkeys and apes have three kinds of colour sensor, with peaks near 430, 539 and 561 nanometres. Some New World monkeys have only two, and the owl monkey has one, so it sees no colour. We show colours the way a person with three kinds of sensor would see them.

A marmoset's fovea is estimated to resolve about 30 cycles per degree, and a rhesus monkey reached 26.3 cycles per degree on a test. Most monkeys and apes are sharper than a person at the centre. We blur the picture to about 10, which is the middle of the measured figures.

Monkeys show direction selectivity in most of the cells of area MT, and 86% of marmoset MT cells respond to the direction of motion. Movement is a strong part of what they see, so the view stresses it.

The width of the sharp middle, the field of view, the gain and the blur at the edge are the app's own picks. No record gives them for these animals, so they are guesses that a person can change in the tuning panel.
Owl monkeys and bushbabies are active at night, and their retinas are built for dim light. Most other monkeys and apes are day-active.

A rhesus monkey reached 26.3 cycles per degree, and a marmoset's cone mosaic could support close to 30. A person sees about 30, so the picture is only slightly softer. A mouse lemur manages about 4.9, which is far blurrier.
Most monkeys have a fovea, a small pit in the retina where cones are packed closely. Squirrel monkeys show it clearly. Owl monkeys have only a rudimentary one.
Cells in the visual cortex of macaques respond to the small differences between the two eyes' views. Diurnal primates use these differences to judge distance among branches.

rows: Whales, dolphins and seals have only one kind of cone or none, so they see little colour. Most of their seeing is done by rod cells, which give a picture of light and dark. A blue-green tint is the closest a phone can show.

Dolphins see a panoramic field of 120 to 130 degrees, and the two eyes overlap only 20 to 30 degrees. We widen the picture to 130 degrees.
Bottlenose dolphins, bowhead whales and other cetaceans carry a reflective layer behind the retina that shows blue-green. We draw a sheen, and a little gain for dim light.
The colour tint, the gate that fades still things, the gain and the sheen strength are the app's own choices, since the records give no figures for them.

rows: An octopus resolves about 12 cycles per degree in one test and a squid about 6.6. A cuttlefish is put at about 8. A person manages about 30, so the screen is blurred to 8 cycles per degree.

Octopus, squid and cuttlefish carry one visual pigment, and tests find no colour vision. Octopus pigments peak between 475 and 487 nanometres. The picture keeps brightness weighted toward blue-green light and loses hue.

A cuttlefish eye covers 253 degrees on the horizontal plane, and a growing oval squid covers 295 to 329 degrees. A cuttlefish can overlap its two eyes in front by 86 degrees. The picture uses 291 degrees, the middle of 253 and 329.
An octopus pupil is round in darkness and narrows to a horizontal slit in bright light.
An octopus retina packs about 55,000 cells per square millimetre into a central horizontal stripe, against 18,000 to 22,000 at the edges. Cuttlefish and squid also have a streak or a centred area.
No reflective layer behind the retina has been found in any squid studied, and none in any cephalopod to date. The picture carries no sheen.
Octopuses tell vertical from horizontal polarized light, and two species respond to differences of about 1.3 degrees in its angle. The picture leaves it out for now.

The one figure of 8 cycles per degree for the whole group, the 291 degree field, the horizontal slit for every animal, the one-pigment colour mapping, and the weights of the sharp stripe are the app's own settings. Squid and cuttlefish pupils are not described in the records, so the octopus slit stands for them.

claims.how: The cuttlefish acuity record states about 8 cycles per degree, and the view uses 8 for the group.
(253 + 329) / 2 = 291 degrees, the middle of the cuttlefish uniocular field and the 35 day squid field.
The octopus pupil constricts to a horizontal slit in bright light, drawn as the horizontal slit shape.
The matrix is built from one pigment peak at 485 nm, the peak stated for Hapalochlaena maculosa and Octopus australis.
No tapetum has been found in cephalopods or squid, so the sheen is 0.
